name: Femi Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Femi. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and what you say stays confidential. Could you walk me through a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive an eight-wheel tipper for a family-run quarry outside town. I'm loading gravel and sand by seven, then running it out to building sites, farm tracks and the odd driveway, maybe six or seven loads a day. I love the sound of a full load sliding off the back in one go. What gets me down is the dust, and customers who swear they ordered twenty tonnes when the ticket says ten.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I've got a little terraced house that I bought three years ago with some help from my dad, and I've got a good bit saved on top. My girlfriend Ruth works at the primary school and we go to the same church on Sundays. I don't use any of these AI programs. My phone does calls, texts and the football scores, and that's enough for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. Every few years there's a new thing that's going to change the world, and the gravel still needs moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life carries on, and I'm glad. The quarry's been going sixty years and it'll go another sixty. There are plenty of tipper jobs around here if it ever closed, so I'm not worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, and keep paying a bit extra off the house each month. Ruth and I would probably get engaged next year. I wouldn't bother learning any computer stuff, because there'd be no need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Settled. That's how I like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the biggest pressure in your life right now, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the price of diesel and what it does to the quarry. Mr Dawson, the owner, mutters about it every Friday. But he's been through worse, and the work keeps coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything change at the quarry office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the girl in the weighbridge office gets a program for the tickets. That's fine by me if it stops the arguments about twenty tonnes and ten. I'd still be the one tipping it.

say: I'd tell people **I told you so** about the hype.
I'd say the **gravel still needs moving** whatever the latest fashion.
think: I think my **life carries on** and I'm glad of it.
With **plenty of tipper jobs** nearby, even a quarry closure wouldn't scare me.
do: Keep driving the **tipper** for the quarry as before.
Pay a bit **extra off the house** each month.
feel: He feels **settled** and content with things staying the same.
S0.quote: Every few years there's a new thing that's going to change the world, and the gravel still needs moving.
fieldNote: He takes a **sceptic's pride** in having expected the hype to fade.
His real pressure is **diesel prices** at the quarry, which he sees as manageable.
He'd welcome **weighbridge software** only if it ends ticket disputes.

steps.text: Keep driving the eight-wheel tipper for the quarry
Pay a little extra off the house mortgage each month
Propose to Ruth next year as planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office types and the computer people who'll feel it, not us. Nobody's writing an app that can back a tipper down a farm track in the rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm not bothered. Mr Dawson won't buy anything that doesn't pay for itself in a year, and a robot tipper won't be cheap. If the paperwork goes to a computer, fine. My bit is my hands and my eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and see what happens. I'd keep the same money habits: savings, a bit off the house. If the quarry made me use a tablet for the tickets I'd learn it, slowly, and probably moan about it at the dinner table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. A bit annoyed by all the fuss on the news, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think is to blame for jobs that do shrink in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big tech companies, mostly, and the people who buy whatever they're selling without thinking. A firm should look after the people who built it. Mr Dawson would, I'll give him that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If a younger driver asked you whether to learn the AI tools, what would you say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn a proper trade first, with your hands, and don't let the computer stuff be the only thing you can do. If you want it on top, fine. That's what my dad told me about phones and I still think he's right.

say: I'd say the **office types** will feel it, not tipper drivers.
I'd say no app can **back a tipper** down a farm track in the rain.
think: I trust the **quarry owner** won't buy robots that don't pay back fast.
I see my work as **hands and eyes**, which software can't touch.
do: Carry on driving and **see what happens** before changing anything.
Keep my **savings habits** and paying extra off the house.
Learn a **ticket tablet** slowly if the quarry insists.
feel: He feels **calm**, though irritated by the news coverage.
S1.quote: Learn a proper trade first, with your hands, and don't let the computer stuff be the only thing you can do.
fieldNote: He places trust in a **cautious, family-run owner** who protects his staff.
He blames **big tech** and careless buyers for any job losses.
His advice to the young echoes **his father's view** on trades over screens.

steps.text: Keep driving the tipper and hold off on any changes
Keep paying extra off the house every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people building these things should be ashamed of themselves, putting working men out of a job with no warning. I'd say it at church, at the pub and anywhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm done driving by about 2031. Something that can drive a tipper and tip it as well as me, that's my job gone. I'd be thirty-two, with a house, and I've never done anything else. It'd keep me up at night, I won't pretend it wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop paying extra off the house and build up cash instead, as much as I could in those few years. I'd talk to my uncle, who runs a small groundworks firm, about starting with him on the diggers, because there's skill in that and it's family. Ruth and I would get married sooner rather than later, while I've got a steady wage to show for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, honestly. Angry too. I did everything right, learned a trade, bought a house, and it wouldn't matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd go to your uncle rather than to a government scheme. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because family looks after family. I don't want a handout, I want a job. My uncle would take me on and teach me properly, the way it should be done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't the diggers be automated too, by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes, and that's what scares me. I'd still rather be on a machine with my uncle for a few more years than sitting at home. Maybe the small firms are the last to buy robots, because they can't afford them.

say: I'd say the builders of AGI should be **ashamed**, ending jobs with no warning.
I'd say it openly at **church** and at the pub.
think: I think I'm **done driving** by about 2031.
At thirty-two with a house and **one trade**, the worry would keep me awake.
do: Stop overpaying the house and **build cash savings** instead.
Ask my uncle about joining his **groundworks firm** on the diggers.
Marry Ruth **sooner** while I have a steady wage.
feel: He feels **frightened** about losing the only work he knows.
He feels **angry** because he did everything right and it wouldn't count.
S2.quote: I did everything right, learned a trade, bought a house, and it wouldn't matter.
fieldNote: He turns to **family, not the state**, for a way out, matching his values.
He knows the **digger plan** may also be automated but prefers work to waiting.
His anger targets **the builders of AI**, framed as a moral failing.

steps.text: Stop overpaying the mortgage and build up cash instead
Ask his uncle about a place on the groundworks diggers
Bring the wedding with Ruth forward while his wage is steady

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for the government and the big firms to do right by working people, and they'd better use it. I'd say a lot about it, probably too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the same ending, just not so soon. The thinking computers in 2031 don't touch my job, but the robots in 2034 do. I'd be thirty-five. That's still a lot of years of mortgage left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and save hard, more than now. I'd wait a few years to see what the first robot lorries are actually like before I jump. If they're rubbish on a muddy site, I'll stay put. If they're good, I'll go to my uncle around 2032.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not like the fast one. I'd have time to think straight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut, to save harder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The new pickup I've had my eye on. And the lads' weekend away in the summer, probably. The house and Ruth come first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see. Is that the right call, with only a few years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not, but I won't throw away a good job on a guess. My dad always said don't cross a bridge until you've seen it. I'd keep watching though, closely.

say: I'd say government and big firms must **do right** by working people.
I'd say they'd better **use the time** they've been given.
think: I think robots by **2034** still end my driving job.
At thirty-five I'd still have **many mortgage years** left.
do: Keep driving and **save harder**, skipping the new pickup.
**Wait** to see how robot lorries handle muddy sites before jumping.
Join my **uncle's firm** around 2032 if the robots prove good.
feel: He feels **worried** but able to think straight with more time.
S3.quote: My dad always said don't cross a bridge until you've seen it.
fieldNote: He chooses **wait and watch** over early action, true to his caution.
His **mortgage** is the main stake that keeps him worried.
His fallback remains **the family firm**, not public schemes.

steps.text: Skip the new pickup and the summer weekend away to save
Watch how the first robot lorries cope on muddy sites
Join his uncle's groundworks firm around 2032 if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of warning and nobody should be crying about it. If you can't sort yourself out in ten years, that's on you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's still a long way off. I'd be thirty-nine by the time a robot can tip gravel. I'd have most of the house paid and maybe a couple of kids by then, so I'd worry about it more for them than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, marry Ruth, and start a family. I'd keep saving and paying off the house. Maybe in my early thirties I'd start doing weekends with my uncle on the diggers, just to have it on my belt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but mostly fine. It's far enough away to get on with life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your own kids about work, in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my kids to learn something with their hands and to stay close to family, same as me. And go to church. Machines don't change what matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'that's on you'. Would you say that to an older driver who couldn't adapt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not to his face. Some of the older lads at the quarry have bad backs and no schooling. I'd want Mr Dawson to look after them. I suppose I'm harder on young people than old ones.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty of warning for anyone.
I'd say people who don't adapt in a decade have **themselves to blame**.
think: I'd be **thirty-nine** before a robot can tip gravel.
I'd worry more for **my kids** than for myself by then.
do: Marry Ruth and **start a family** on the current wage.
Keep **saving** and paying off the house.
Do **weekend digger work** with my uncle in my early thirties.
feel: He feels **slightly uneasy** but mostly fine getting on with life.
S4.quote: I'd tell my kids to learn something with their hands and to stay close to family, same as me.
fieldNote: His public line is **tough on adaptability**, softened when asked about older drivers.
He shifts his concern to **the next generation** when the timeline is long.
His plans centre on **marriage and children**, not career change.

steps.text: Marry Ruth and start a family as planned
Keep paying down the house and saving steadily
Do weekend shifts on his uncle's diggers in his early thirties

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028. I've got a house and I'm about to start a family, and three or four years isn't long enough to start again. What would help is apprenticeships for grown men, paid by the firms that make the robots, not handouts. Let us learn a new trade properly, on the job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about pride. Driving a tipper isn't just a wage to me. When I drop a load right where the builder wants it, first time, that's something I did. A machine doing it better doesn't take that pride away, but it'd take away the reason to get up at six.

headlineQuote: A machine doing it better doesn't take that pride away, but it'd take away the reason to get up at six.
portrait: Femi is a **27-year-old tipper driver** for a family-run quarry, with a house and solid savings.
He goes to **church with Ruth**, his girlfriend, and never uses AI tools.
He's **calm** in AI Plateau and Steady Disruption, trusting a cautious owner and hands-on work.
In AGI by 2028 he's **alarmed**, turning to his uncle's groundworks firm rather than the state.
With more time he **waits and watches**, putting marriage and children first.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** most, because a house and a new family leave no time to restart.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **paid apprenticeships** for adults, funded by robot makers, not handouts.
